title: Emilia-Romagna
quiz.0.question: What is the mainstream modern style of quality Lambrusco?
quiz.0.explanation: Classic Lambrusco is dry (sometimes off-dry); the sweet, characterless versions made for export markets in the 1970s-80s were nothing like what Italians drink themselves.
quiz.1.question: Ranking Lambrusco di Sorbara, Grasparossa and Salamino from lightest to fullest:
quiz.1.explanation: Sorbara is the classic, lightest version in colour, body, alcohol and structure; Salamino is often described as the most balanced, in between; Grasparossa is the fullest, most concentrated and most tannic.
quiz.2.question: What is Lambrusco’s “metodo ancestrale” also called?
quiz.2.options.1: Rifermentazione naturale in bottiglia (natural re-fermentation in bottle)
quiz.2.explanation: The ancestral method is also commonly called rifermentazione naturale in bottiglia; like the traditional method it is a small share, usually reserved for the finest, more layered wines. The vast majority of Lambrusco is made by the tank method.
quiz.3.question: What is the legal minimum ageing for Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale di Modena or di Reggio Emilia?
quiz.3.explanation: Tradizionale must age at least 12 years by law, moved through progressively smaller barrels of different woods in a Solera-like system; the genuine product carries the DOP logo.
slides.0.title: Emilia-Romagna
slides.0.subtitle: Lambrusco · Romagna Albana DOCG · Balsamic vinegar · Italy’s food heartland
slides.1.title: Italy’s Food Heartland — Emilia vs Romagna
slides.1.content:
Emilia-Romagna is one of the wealthiest regions in Italy and Europe, famous for Lambrusco, Parmigiano Reggiano, Prosciutto di Parma and Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale. Yet “Emilia” and “Romagna” are two very different places: locals identify as either Emiliani or Romagnoli, never both.

Emilia (west and centre)

Provinces: Piacenza, Parma, Reggio Emilia, Modena, Ferrara and most of Bologna
Identity: historically considered part of northern Italy
Style: mainly frizzante (semi-sparkling) wines, with more varied appellations
Signatures: Lambrusco, Colli Piacentini, Colli Bolognesi Pignoletto DOCG

Romagna (south-east)

Provinces: Ravenna, Forlì-Cesena, Rimini
Identity: feels kinship with central Italy
Style: mainly still wines, mostly under the large Romagna DOC
Signatures: Romagna Sangiovese, Romagna Albana DOCG

A world-class food map

Parmigiano Reggiano
Prosciutto di Parma
Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale (Modena / Reggio Emilia)
Tortellini and other handmade pasta
Mortadella (Bologna)
Piadina (Romagna flatbread)

slides.3.title: 📜 History and Terroir (IWS)
slides.3.content:
From the Celts to the Kingdom of Italy: two thousand years of history

Emilia-Romagna’s native peoples were Celts; before the Romans invaded in the 3rd-2nd centuries BC, locals were already growing vines under Etruscan tutelage. In the 1st century BC Pliny the Elder recorded the fizzy white wines around Bologna and the fizzy reds made from Lambrusche (Lambrusco) grapes on the plain around Modena — the earliest written record of Lambrusco. A century later the Roman consul Marco Emilio Lepido built the Via Emilia from Piacenza in the west to Rimini on the Adriatic, a trade route that eventually gave the region its name.

After the fall of Rome in the 5th century the region split into Emilia (under the Lombards, developing city-states such as Parma, Piacenza, Modena, Reggio Emilia and Bologna) and Romagna (first under the Byzantines, who called it “Romania” — the origin of “Romagna” — then, after Pippin the Short helped the Pope defeat the Lombards, part of the Papal States until Napoléon’s invasion in the late 18th century). After the 1815 Congress of Vienna the old order briefly returned; following the 1860 plebiscites both joined the Kingdom of Sardegna (the Kingdom of Italy a year later), yet Emiliani and Romagnoli still see their dialects, food and culture as different. The Alma Mater Studiorum, founded in Bologna in 1088, is the oldest university in the western world.

Topography, climate and soils

Three bands: plains 48% (the Po valley, ancient marine sediments plus river alluvium, deep and fertile, with two-thirds of the vineyard area), hills 27% (naturally shallow soils of clay, sandstone and marl — poor soils better suited to quality) and mountains 25% (the Northern Apennines, rarely above 2,000 m, with no vines)
A climate spectrum: the plains are continental (hot, humid summers, long cold winters) and the driest part, with only 20-30 in/600-800 mm of rain and frequent autumn and winter fog; the hills are semi-continental (more rain, cooler summers, milder winters); the coast is Mediterranean, with sea breezes moderating temperatures year-round
The Po’s double edge: the Po and its many tributaries (Panaro, Secchia, Taro, Trebbia) moderate the climate overall, but also raise humidity and the risk of mould and rot — the main challenge for vineyards on the plain
Scale: over 123,000 acres/50,000 ha of vineyards (8% of Italy) and about 6 million hl a year (10% of Italy); as of 2017 there are 21 appellations (19 DOCs and 2 DOCGs), DOC/DOCG is about 25% of production, IGT 40% (mainly Emilia IGT and Rubicone IGT), and the rest generic wine
Cooperatives: vineyards are split into countless small plots averaging just 5 acres/2 ha; more than two-thirds of growers (with 60% of the vineyard area) belong to cooperatives, which make 85% of the region’s wine — among Italy’s largest cooperative networks; yet the best and most interesting wines mostly come from independent estates in the hills of Emilia and Romagna
slides.4.title: Lambrusco — From Export Sweetness to Local Classic
slides.4.content:
Lambrusco’s two faces

In the 1970s and 1980s Emilia-Romagna was famous for Lambrusco: a sweet, slightly fizzy, undistinguished red crafted for sugar-loving export markets and nothing like the Lambrusco Italians drank. Its international success was a double-edged sword — it brought wealth but cemented the region’s image as a mass-producer of uninspiring wine. From the end of the 20th century, more and more quality-minded small estates emerged, especially in the Lambrusco district and the hills of Piacenza, Bologna and Romagna.

Classic DOC Lambrusco

What the locals drink

Hallmark: a mushroom cork

Style: dry (sometimes off-dry), with a pink foam when poured, refreshing acidity, bright red fruit, floral notes and minerality

Alcohol and tannin

A light table wine

Alcohol: 10-12%

Tannin: light; both quality levels are meant to be drunk young and lightly chilled

Sweet export Lambrusco

The mass-produced export version

Labelling: usually IGT, with a screw cap

Style: low in alcohol, sweet, fizzy and characterless
slides.5.title: How Lambrusco Is Made
slides.5.content:
Tank method

The vast majority of Lambrusco

Process: second fermentation in a sealed pressure tank
Share: the vast majority of Lambrusco is made this way
Style: mostly frizzante (semi-sparkling), fresh and fruity
Best: drunk young and lightly chilled

Metodo ancestrale

A few top wines

Also called: rifermentazione naturale in bottiglia (natural re-fermentation in bottle)
Process: re-fermentation is completed in the bottle
Style: extra complexity, with savoury, balsamic and mineral notes
Use: usually reserved for the finest bottlings

Metodo Classico

A few top wines

Process: second fermentation in bottle
Share: only a small proportion
Style: like the ancestral method, it adds extra layers
Key point: the best Lambruscos are never expensive
slides.6.title: The Main Lambrusco DOCs
slides.6.content:
#1

Lambrusco di Sorbara DOC

Location: around the hamlet of Sorbara, including the city of Modena and the plain to its north and north-east

Grapes: at least 60% Lambrusco di Sorbara, up to 40% Lambrusco Salamino

Style: the lightest Lambrusco in colour, body, alcohol and structure — the classic benchmark

Flavours: red fruit, pink grapefruit, violets

Character: elegant, high in acidity, dry or off-dry; wines from the hillier land south of Modena are more structured

Viticulture: Sorbara needs another Lambrusco as a pollinator, usually interplanted Salamino

#2

Lambrusco Grasparossa di Castelvetro DOC

Location: the hills around Castelvetro, south of Modena at the foot of the Northern Apennines

Grape: Lambrusco Grasparossa (the second most planted Lambrusco)

Style: the fullest and most concentrated, with a deeper purple-red colour

Flavours: red and black fruit, flowers, an earthy note and a touch of balsamic

Character: higher acidity and a noticeable tannic grip; any residual sugar balances tannin and acidity; often considered among the best Lambruscos on the market

#3

Lambrusco Salamino di Santa Croce DOC

Location: around the hamlet of Santa Croce on the plain north of Modena, north of the Sorbara DOC

Name: the bunches look like small salami (salamino)

Standing: Lambrusco Salamino is the most widely planted Lambrusco

Style: often called the most balanced, between Sorbara and Grasparossa; usually dry

#4

Reggiano DOC

Location: the plain north and the hills south of Reggio Emilia

Wines: a rosso based on Ancellotta and Lambrusco, Lambrusco blends, varietal Lambrusco Salamino and more

Style: Reggiano Lambrusco is among the lightest, easiest-drinking Lambruscos

Character: one of the most widely produced and exported Lambrusco DOCs
slides.7.title: 🍷 Label Example: Lambrusco Grasparossa di Castelvetro
slides.7.caption: Tenuta Pederzana “il Grasparossa della tradizione” — Lambrusco Grasparossa di Castelvetro DOC, Vino Frizzante Semi secco (off-dry semi-sparkling), 12% vol, estate-bottled by a grower in the Castelvetro hills.
slides.8.title: Leading Lambrusco Producers
slides.8.content:
Cleto Chiarli — a historic house

Founded: 1860, Modena
Signature: Vigneto Enrico Cialdini (Lambrusco Grasparossa di Castelvetro)
Known for: one of the oldest Lambrusco houses, keeping Modena’s dry tradition alive

Alberto Paltrinieri — the Sorbara specialist

Location: Sorbara
Signature: Radice (Lambrusco di Sorbara, natural re-fermentation in bottle)
Known for: a focus on Lambrusco di Sorbara, with top wines made by the ancestral and traditional methods

Hillside Lambrusco

Key point: hill Lambruscos are fuller-bodied and more structured, more mineral, spicy and tannic
Examples: Grasparossa growers in the Castelvetro hills, and hillside Lambrusco from Colli di Scandiano e di Canossa
Standing: Lambruscos from hillside vineyards are considered among the finest made

Large cooperatives and houses

Standing: cooperatives make 85% of the region’s wine, and some are among Italy’s largest
Examples: Cavicchioli (1928, Modena), Riunite and others
Known for: large volumes of Lambrusco from plain-grown grapes; some also make single-vineyard wines
slides.9.title: Romagna Albana DOCG — Italy’s First White DOCG
slides.9.content:
1987: a controversial “first”

Romagna Albana (formerly Albana di Romagna) was Emilia-Romagna’s first DOCG and, more controversially, Italy’s first white DOCG. Its promotion in 1987 was widely disputed, as the wine was little known outside Romagna and most did not think it worthy of the honour; producers have since worked hard to prove otherwise.

1987: Italy’s first white DOCG | Area: the hilly band east of Bologna towards the Adriatic | Best: Bertinoro

Five styles (all still)

Secco (dry): well-structured and lightly tannic, with the typical vegetal-sage aroma plus floral, stone fruit and almond notes; dry versions are improving and becoming more common, often from single vineyards and increasingly barrel-aged
Amabile (medium-dry to medium-sweet) and Dolce (sweet): traditional sweetness levels
Passito: the most impressive Romagna Albana wines are still the passitos; the technique suits the grape particularly well, often with added layers from noble rot
Passito Riserva: higher minimum potential alcohol and at least 1 year of ageing; the best come from Bertinoro, a village with a long Albana passito tradition
slides.10.title: 🍇 More Native Grapes and Industry Data (IWS)
slides.10.content:
Is Sangiovese not Tuscan after all?

Recent DNA research has shown Sangiovese to be a natural cross of two southern Italian grapes — Ciliegiolo and the almost extinct Calabrese (Montenuovo) — and related to several other southern grapes, suggesting a southern rather than Tuscan origin. Interestingly, some of the finest Sangiovese clones grown in Toscana today actually came from Romagna. Legend says the name comes from the Latin “sanguis Jovi” (Jupiter’s blood), given by monks near Monte Giove close to Rimini in Romagna.

Most widely planted grapes (ISTAT, 2010): Trebbiano Romagnolo 28% · Sangiovese 15% · Lambrusco Salamino 8% · Ancellotta 7% · Lambrusco Grasparossa 4% · Barbera 4% · Croatina 3% · Pignoletto 3% · Lambrusco di Sorbara 3% · Albana 2% · Others 23%

Native white grapes of the Piacenza / Parma hills

Malvasia di Candia Aromatica: an aromatic grape widely grown across Emilia and especially championed in the Piacenza and Parma hills; made still, sparkling and passito, and its passitos are considered among Italy’s best
Ortrugo: native to the Piacenza hills and grown there for centuries, though not documented until the 19th century; the name comes from the dialect Altruga (“the other grape”). It nearly vanished in the 20th century and has been bottled as a varietal since the 1970s; it is now one of the most planted whites in the Piacenza hills, crisp and mineral
Spergola: a native white of the Scandiano / Canossa hills in Reggio Emilia province, bottled still or frizzante and from dry to sweet

Other native red grapes

Ancellotta (often used to add colour to Lambrusco blends) · Barbera · Bonarda (Croatina) · Fortana (the red of the Bosco Eliceo sands) · Malbo Gentile · Terrano (used for Cagnina) · Barbarossa
A Lambrusco curiosity: Lambrusco di Sorbara needs another Lambrusco variety interplanted as a pollinator, usually Lambrusco Salamino; hence the Lambrusco di Sorbara DOC requires at least 60% Sorbara and at most 40% Salamino. Other minor Lambruscos include Lambrusco Marani and Lambrusco Maestri.
slides.11.title: Romagna Sangiovese and the Romagna DOC
slides.11.content:
Romagna’s signature red

Sangiovese and Trebbiano Romagnolo together cover more than 40% of Emilia-Romagna’s vineyards. The Romagna DOC, created in 2011, brought five previously independent appellations together; Romagna Sangiovese is its popular and quantitatively important wine, and can be made as superiore, riserva and novello.

Romagna Sangiovese | 12 sub-zones | Sub-zones: 95% Sangiovese (vs 85%), lower yields, slightly higher minimum alcohol

Compared with Tuscan Sangiovese

Romagna style: the best examples tend to be rounder, less acidic and softer in tannin than their Tuscan counterparts; exemplary bottlings can age well and gain complexity
Sangiovese’s origins: DNA has shown it to be a natural cross of Ciliegiolo and Calabrese (Montenuovo), probably from the south; some of Toscana’s finest Sangiovese clones actually came from Romagna

Leading producers

San Patrignano: the winery of a drug-rehabilitation community near Rimini; its signature is Avi (Romagna Sangiovese Riserva)
Tre Monti: a family estate in the Imola hills, known for Romagna Sangiovese and Albana
Fattoria Zerbina: an estate near Faenza, known for Romagna Sangiovese and Albana passito
slides.12.title: Trebbiano Romagnolo and Aceto Balsamico
slides.12.content:
Trebbiano Romagnolo is Emilia-Romagna’s most planted grape (28%), used as a blending component in several appellations, though Romagna producers in particular champion it as a varietal. It is also linked to Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale, whose grape must comes from Lambrusco or Trebbiano Romagnolo.

Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale DOP — Emilia’s most traditional treasure

Where: made only in Reggio Emilia and Modena, with Modena usually considered the more prestigious
Process: Lambrusco or Trebbiano Romagnolo must is boiled down to a sweet syrup and fermented to 4-5% alcohol; it then goes into small barrels left partly empty, slowly turning to vinegar through oxidation and evaporation, and is moved through progressively smaller barrels of different woods (oak, cherry, acacia, chestnut and others) kept in draughty lofts, managed much like the Solera of Jerez
Ageing: at least 12 years by law; the extravecchio (extra-old) version is aged longer
Tradizionale vs everyday: genuine Tradizionale carries the DOP logo; ordinary Aceto Balsamico (without the word Tradizionale) is a mass-produced product of simple vinegar sweetened and coloured with caramel, and far cheaper

Romagna Trebbiano — the wine itself

Made still, semi-sparkling or sparkling, dry or off-dry, often with some Trebbiano Toscano (the two are often interplanted). Light and fresh for early drinking, it is the local everyday white, traditionally drunk in the seafood restaurants of the Riviera Romagnola
Trebbiano Romagnolo is an ancient grape making simple, refreshing wines
slides.13.title: Colli Bolognesi & Pignoletto DOCG
slides.13.content:
The Bologna hills — home of Grechetto (Pignoletto)

The Bologna district covers the plains north and west of the city and the hills to the south, and the white Grechetto (Pignoletto) is its most distinctive grape. DNA profiling has shown it to be identical to Grechetto di Todi, a traditional Umbrian grape. Colli Bolognesi Pignoletto DOCG is one of Emilia-Romagna’s two DOCGs, with vineyards in the hills south-west of Bologna, the grape’s historic home; it was split from the Colli Bolognesi DOC and promoted in 2010.

Since 2014 the grape has been called Grechetto (Grechetto Gentile) rather than Pignoletto; “Pignoletto” now names the historic production area around Monteveglio near Bologna

The style of Grechetto (Pignoletto)

Flavours: typically light-bodied, with white flowers, citrus and apple
Texture: the substantial tannin in its skins adds an appealing texture
Uses: high acidity makes it suitable for sparkling and late-harvest wines

Other Colli Bolognesi wines

Barbera: a varietal Italian grape in the Colli Bolognesi DOC
International grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay account for some of the district’s most impressive wines
slides.14.title: 🏞️ The Appellations of the Piacenza, Parma and Reggio Emilia Hills
slides.14.content:
Western Emilia: four districts along the Via Emilia

Emilia’s appellations fall into four successive districts running north-west to south-east along the Via Emilia from Piacenza to Bologna: the Piacenza hills, the Parma hills, the Lambrusco district of Reggio Emilia and Modena, and the Bologna district. The Piacenza hills were planted by the Etruscans and share growing conditions with the neighbouring Oltrepò Pavese hills in Lombardia, rising to 650-1,600 ft/200-500 m in a series of parallel valleys.

Colli Piacentini DOC and its four sub-zones

Colli Piacentini DOC: one of Emilia’s largest and most productive districts. Reds are mainly Barbera and Bonarda (Croatina), often semi-sparkling; whites are mainly Malvasia di Candia Aromatica (labelled Colli Piacentini Malvasia DOC), traditionally aromatic, off-dry and semi-sparkling, with passitos also traditional; a Vin Santo from Malvasia and Ortrugo is allowed
Three blended sub-zones: Monterosso Val d'Arda, Trebbianino Val Trebbia and Valnure, blending Malvasia di Candia Aromatica, Ortrugo and Trebbiano Romagnolo, from dry to semi-sweet and still to frizzante or sparkling
Vin Santo di Vigoleno: the fourth sub-zone, an ancient sweet passito from the native white grapes Santa Maria and Melara grown around the medieval town of Vigoleno; it must age at least 4 years in oak, developing candied fruit, honey, nuts and tamarind

Two DOCs that went their own way: Gutturnio and Ortrugo

Gutturnio DOC: a Barbera and Bonarda (Croatina) blend that became its own DOC in 2010, split from Colli Piacentini; the name comes from the Roman jug (gutturnium) found near Piacenza in 1878. Traditionally frizzante (dry or slightly sweet); superiore needs higher minimum alcohol, and riserva at least 2 years’ ageing (6 months in oak); classico is reserved for the historic zone at superiore or riserva level, all still and dry
Ortrugo DOC: its own DOC for Ortrugo, with exactly the same borders as Colli Piacentini DOC, made still, frizzante or semi-dry
Colli di Parma DOC: the hills west and south of Parma, mostly frizzante, from native and international grapes; the most distinctive use Lambrusco Maestri, Barbera, Malvasia di Candia Aromatica and Sauvignon Blanc

The Reggio Emilia hills: Colli di Scandiano e di Canossa DOC

South-west of Reggio Emilia, with both plain and hills; most wines are frizzante. The most distinctive are based on the native white Spergola (still or frizzante, dry to sweet); other key wines are Malvasia, Lambrusco Grasparossa, Lambrusco Montericco, Malbo Gentile, Cabernet Sauvignon and Sauvignon Blanc. Lambruscos from this DOC’s hillside vineyards are considered among the finest of all.
slides.15.title: 🏛️ Bologna and the Romagna Hills: The Full DOC Structure
slides.15.content:
The Bologna district: Colli Bolognesi DOC and Reno DOC

Colli Bolognesi DOC (the base): in the hills south and south-west of Bologna, and separate from the Colli Bolognesi Pignoletto DOCG — it focuses on red and white blends plus varietal Barbera and international grapes such as Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay, with a smaller “Bologna” sub-zone mainly for red and white blends
Reno DOC: white wine only, covering the plains north and east of Bologna and the land between Bologna and Modena: a varietal Montù, Reno Bianco (Trebbiano Romagnolo plus Albana) and the most popular, Reno Montuni (still, frizzante or spumante, dry to sweet, high in acidity, light, with flowers and unripe citrus)
Pignoletto DOC (new in 2014): distinct from the Colli Bolognesi Pignoletto DOCG, it regulates varietal Pignoletto wines from around Bologna plus nearby villages in Modena and Ravenna provinces, with three sub-zones (Modena, Reno, Colli d'Imola); still, frizzante, spumante, passito and late-harvest styles; at least 85% Grechetto (Pignoletto), and still superiore wines from the historic area may be labelled classico with at least 95%

Romagna DOC (2011): an umbrella of five sub-designations

The Romagna DOC, created in 2011, turned five previously independent appellations into sub-designations; “Romagna” must appear before each on the label: ① Sangiovese (the main focus of this course, with 12 sub-zones requiring 95%), ② Trebbiano (mainly Trebbiano Romagnolo), ③ Pagadebit (from Bombino Bianco, whose synonym means “pays the debts” for its reliable crops even in bad years; one sub-zone, Bertinoro; still or frizzante, dry or medium-sweet), ④ Cagnina (the autumn sweet red covered in this course) and ⑤ Albana Spumante (a sparkling wine from partly dried Albana, tank or traditional method, with the same zone as Romagna Albana DOCG)

The minor Romagna hill appellations and Bosco Eliceo DOC

Four hill appellations: from west to east across the hills from Bologna to Rimini on the Adriatic — Colli d'Imola DOC, Colli di Faenza DOC, Colli Romagna Centrale DOC and Colli di Rimini DOC — each focused on native and international grapes (Trebbiano Romagnolo, Sangiovese, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon), as red or white blends and varietals
Bosco Eliceo DOC: a narrow strip of sandy coast along the Po delta south of Ravenna, with up to 95-97% sand, where phylloxera cannot survive, so many vines are ungrafted — hence “vini delle sabbie” (wines of the sands). Its flagship is Bosco Eliceo Fortana, from the rare native red Fortana (locally “uva d'oro”, the golden grape), still, vivace or frizzante, dry to sweet, traditionally paired with local eels
slides.16.title: Romagna Cagnina
slides.16.content:
Romagna Cagnina — the autumn new wine

Grape: made from Terrano, known for its mouth-cleansing tannic bite
Style: a sweet red
Release: in October following the harvest, best drunk fresh
Tradition: locals drink it as soon as it is released, with roasted chestnuts; Cagnina is one of the five sub-designations of the Romagna DOC
slides.17.title: Lambrusco and Emilian Food
slides.17.content:
Why is Lambrusco the perfect partner for Emilian food?

High acidity — cuts through rich food based on pasta, cheese, cream, butter and cured meats
Bubbles — refresh the palate
Low alcohol (10-12%) — never overwhelms the food
Light tannins — and, by common belief, an aid to digestion

Classic pairings

Lambrusco di Sorbara (lightest)
  • Fried seafood (fritto di mare)
  • Prosciutto di Parma
  • Piadina flatbread
  • Light salads
Lambrusco Salamino / Reggiano (medium)
  • Tagliatelle al ragù
  • Parmigiano Reggiano
  • A mortadella platter
  • Pizza
Lambrusco Grasparossa (fullest)
  • Zampone / cotechino sausages
  • Aged Parmigiano Reggiano
  • Grilled red meat
  • Parmigiana di melanzane (aubergine bake)
slides.18.title: Key Takeaways
slides.18.points.0: Emilia (west) focuses on frizzante wines with more varied appellations; Romagna (south-east) on still wines, mostly under the Romagna DOC
slides.18.points.1: Scale: over 50,000 ha of vineyards (8% of Italy) and about 6 million hl a year (10% of Italy); cooperatives make 85% of production; DOC/DOCG is about 25%
slides.18.points.2: As of 2017 there are 21 appellations: 19 DOCs and 2 DOCGs (Romagna Albana, Colli Bolognesi Pignoletto)
slides.18.points.3: Emilia’s four districts follow the Via Emilia: the Piacenza hills → the Parma hills → the Lambrusco district (Reggio Emilia, Modena) → Bologna
slides.18.points.4: Three key Lambruscos: Sorbara (lightest, needs a pollinator), Salamino (most planted, most balanced), Grasparossa (Castelvetro hills, fullest); Sorbara DOC needs at least 60% Sorbara and at most 40% Salamino
slides.18.points.5: Classic Lambrusco is dry (sometimes off-dry), 10-12% ABV, with pink foam; the vast majority is tank method, a small share traditional or ancestral (natural re-fermentation in bottle)
slides.18.points.6: Romagna Albana DOCG (1987) was Italy’s first white DOCG; its finest wines are passitos, the best from Bertinoro
slides.18.points.7: The Romagna DOC (2011) brings together Sangiovese, Trebbiano, Pagadebit, Cagnina and Albana Spumante; Romagna Sangiovese has 12 sub-zones (95% Sangiovese)
slides.18.points.8: Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale (Modena, Reggio Emilia) must age at least 12 years by law and carries the DOP logo
slides.18.points.9: Bosco Eliceo’s soils are up to 95-97% sand, where phylloxera cannot survive; it is known for Fortana

slides.19.questions.3.explanation: Tradizionale must age at least 12 years by law, moved through progressively smaller barrels of different woods in a Solera-like system; the genuine product carries the DOP logo.
slides.19.questions.4.question: What is the historical significance of Romagna Albana (formerly Albana di Romagna)?
slides.19.questions.4.options.1: In 1987 it became Italy’s first white DOCG
slides.19.questions.4.explanation: Romagna Albana was Emilia-Romagna’s first DOCG and Italy’s first white DOCG; its promotion in 1987 was controversial. Its most impressive wines are passitos, the best from Bertinoro.
slides.19.questions.5.question: What are the grape rules for Lambrusco di Sorbara DOC?
slides.19.questions.5.options.1: At least 60% Sorbara, up to 40% Salamino
slides.19.questions.5.explanation: Lambrusco di Sorbara needs another Lambrusco variety as a pollinator, usually Salamino; the DOC therefore requires at least 60% Sorbara and at most 40% Salamino.
slides.19.questions.6.question: What is Romagna Cagnina?
slides.19.questions.6.options.1: A sweet red from Terrano, released in October after the harvest
slides.19.questions.6.explanation: Cagnina is a sweet red made from Terrano, released in October after the harvest and best drunk fresh; locals enjoy it with roasted chestnuts.
slides.19.questions.7.question: Why are many Bosco Eliceo DOC vines ungrafted?
slides.19.questions.7.options.1: B. The soil is up to 95-97% sand, where phylloxera cannot survive
slides.19.questions.7.options.2: C. The vineyards are too high
slides.19.questions.7.options.3: D. The vines are all new
slides.19.questions.7.explanation: Bosco Eliceo lies on sandy land along the Po delta coast, up to 95-97% sand, where phylloxera cannot survive, so many vines are ungrafted; its wines are called vini delle sabbie (wines of the sands).
slides.19.questions.8.question: DNA profiling has shown Grechetto (Pignoletto) to be identical to which grape?
slides.19.questions.8.explanation: The Grechetto (Pignoletto) of the Bologna hills is identical to Umbria’s traditional Grechetto di Todi; since 2014 the grape has been called Grechetto, while Pignoletto names the historic production area.
slides.19.questions.9.question: Which two grapes are blended in Gutturnio DOC?
slides.19.questions.9.explanation: Gutturnio is a Barbera and Bonarda (Croatina) blend that became its own DOC in 2010, split from Colli Piacentini; its name comes from the Roman jug (gutturnium) found near Piacenza in 1878.
